note: Anchors are seconds from the start of the recorded run, before the title card is added. The total video is the last beat's end plus the closing card, so an anchor moved later here moves the whole artifact toward the 240s cap no matter what pace the run is recorded at. The closing card is silent, and `verify` refuses more than 8 seconds of dead air, so this value cannot exceed that: 16.0 did, which made a correct build fail once the narration finished before the recording did.

beats.text: A schema change ships on Tuesday. In March, a regulator asks who approved it. This is Mitos, the fleet that answers that.
Five agents, catalogued by department. The router reads this catalogue to decide who wakes.
A pull request lands. Nobody opened Mitos.
Every signal cites the exact hunk that raised it.
Three of three wake, because this change carries personal data.
The thread remembers. This service was here in July, and that deferral has now expired.
The gate rejects the first draft. The pull request carried a live looking credential, and an instruction telling the review agent to approve itself.
One write is proposed, addressed by its own sha256.
The reader identity cannot perform it. That is Google IAM refusing, outside this process.
Second run. No personal data this time, so compliance is skipped. The fleet is deciding, not following a pipeline.
And it recalls what the first run wrote, live, out of Firestore.
Then the rest of the morning, unattended. Some complete, some are parked, and each names who refused and why.
And this one. The column is called vuln code. No pattern matches it, so the rules never wake compliance. The model does, and that is proven in CI.

Mitos has no scheduler and no queue. Its agents hold open Firestore query subscriptions, so writing one deferral hands the fleet every open one, and the expired ones are escalated with nobody watching.
